mstts:express-as.prosody: Have you ever wondered why, even with the best intentions, misunderstandings or conflicts can pop up in your relationships? Sometimes, it’s not the words we say, but the invisible forces at play—those subtle, unconscious biases that quietly shape the way we see and connect with others. Together, we’re about to explore this fascinating world of hidden patterns with the help of Gleb Tsipursky’s book, The Blindspots Between Us: How to Overcome Unconscious Cognitive Bias and Build Better Relationships. This isn’t just about theory or abstract ideas. Instead, we’ll dive into real, everyday ways these mental shortcuts can cloud our judgment, create distance, and sometimes keep true empathy just out of reach. But here’s the good news: recognizing and understanding these blindspots is the first step toward building stronger, more authentic connections. Imagine what could happen if we learned to spot those hidden biases—not only in ourselves, but in the people around us. By shining a light on what’s been invisible, we open up new possibilities for trust, compassion, and genuine communication. So, as we set out on this journey together, get ready to discover practical tools and fresh insights for transforming your relationships—one conversation, and one moment of awareness, at a time. Let’s see how bringing these blindspots into the open can help us all connect a little more deeply, and maybe even change the way we see the world.

Chapter 1. Recognizing the Hidden Patterns That Shape Perception
You know, every one of us goes through life with a set of invisible filters—kind of like mental shortcuts and assumptions that quietly shape how we see and understand the world. These are called cognitive biases. They're not a sign of weakness or a lack of intelligence; honestly, they're just a natural part of how our minds try to make sense of all the information flying at us every day.
Think of cognitive bias like wearing a pair of tinted glasses. You can still see everything around you, but the colors are just a little different. These filters work behind the scenes, influencing the way you judge situations, how you react, and even what you remember.
For example, when you meet someone new, your mind instantly starts sorting through details like how they look, how they sound, or the way they carry themselves. Past experiences and cultural cues all play a role. It helps you move through social situations quickly, but—here’s the catch—it can also lead to misunderstandings, or keep you from truly connecting with someone new.
And it’s not just about obvious stereotypes or big, glaring prejudices. There’s a whole collection of mental habits at play, like:
Confirmation bias—this is when you naturally notice and remember things that back up what you already believe, while brushing off anything that doesn’t fit.
Or attribution error—that’s when you chalk up someone else’s actions to their personality, but if you do the same thing, you blame it on the situation.
And then there’s in-group favoritism—feeling drawn to people who seem like you, and maybe, without realizing it, keeping your distance from those who seem different.
These patterns run deep. Most of us pick them up as kids, and they get reinforced by family, culture, media—you name it. It’s not like anyone chooses these blindspots, but here’s the good news: once you notice them, you can do something about it.
The first real step is just admitting that everyone—yes, everyone—has blindspots. There are places where our perception is limited or just a bit off. But don’t beat yourself up about it. Instead, see it as an invitation to get curious.
Picture this: you’re at a family dinner, and suddenly there’s a heated debate about politics. Everyone’s convinced they’re making perfect sense, and nobody can understand why the others don’t agree. Beneath it all, each person is pulling from different life stories, personal values, and hidden assumptions. The conversation stalls—not because anyone's being stubborn, but because these hidden biases are quietly doing their thing.
When you start to spot these patterns, you give yourself a chance to pause before reacting. You can ask, "What might I be missing here?" That tiny moment of self-reflection can open the door to more honest, compassionate conversations.
And really, that's the foundation for growing deeper, more meaningful relationships with the people around you.

prosody.p: Chapter Two: How Bias Shapes Communication and Fuels Misunderstandings.

So, once we recognize that cognitive bias is always in the background, it’s a lot easier to see how it sneaks into our daily conversations. Bias isn’t just a distant concept—it’s like a filter over what we say, and more importantly, what we hear. This is why even well-meaning chats can suddenly feel confusing, or even spark a little conflict. Sometimes, our assumptions quietly take over, and things just go sideways.

You know, communication isn’t just throwing words back and forth. It’s more like a dance—there are signals, little interpretations, and all sorts of emotional undercurrents. Bias plays a part in every single step. Imagine someone giving you feedback. Because of past experiences, or maybe a few insecurities, your brain might instantly hear it as criticism. The real message? It gets buried beneath a defensive reaction.

Picture this at work: a manager offers a suggestion, hoping to help. But the employee, already feeling undervalued, hears nothing but disapproval. The manager’s left scratching their head at the chilly response, and both walk away thinking, “What just happened?” In the end, both feel misunderstood. And if this keeps happening, it can quietly chip away at trust in the relationship.

There are a few common biases that really shape these moments. For example—there’s negativity bias, where our minds latch onto criticism and almost ignore any praise. Then there’s projection bias, where we assume other people must think and feel just like we do, so we totally misread their intentions. And don’t forget the halo effect, where one good—or bad—trait colors our whole view of someone.

Most of the time, these biases aren’t obvious. They might show up as a gut feeling—maybe you’re uneasy about a neighbor for no clear reason, or you jump to conclusions about a coworker’s motives. If we don’t notice these patterns, they can slowly push us apart and erode trust.

So, how do we deal with this? Well, it starts with slowing down and paying attention to the stories our minds are spinning. Are we assuming we know what someone meant? Are we jumping to conclusions with hardly any information? If we gently challenge these automatic reactions, we open up space for a more accurate—and kinder—understanding.

Here’s what can really help: first, pause before you respond. Give yourself a moment to check in with your own feelings. Next, try clarifying intentions—ask open-ended questions to really get where the other person’s coming from. And finally, reflect back what you’ve heard. Summarize it in your own words, just to make sure you’ve got it right.

These small shifts can totally transform conversations. Instead of spiraling into conflict, you’ll find opportunities for real connection. And over time, these habits build trust—a trust that lets you explore differences together, instead of avoiding them.

Chapter 3: Building Self-Awareness as the Foundation for Change
So, recognizing bias is just the starting point. The real journey? It’s about building self-awareness—the ability to watch your own thoughts, feelings, and reactions with honest curiosity. Think of self-awareness like a spotlight, shining into the quiet corners of your mind where bias can hide out.
Now, here’s something to keep in mind: this practice isn’t about beating yourself up or feeling guilty. It’s about showing yourself a gentle, nonjudgmental attention. Imagine how a gardener checks the soil before planting anything. That’s what self-awareness is—just noticing the mental environment where your relationships grow.
So, how do you actually build self-awareness? One of the best ways is mindful reflection. This means pausing to notice patterns in your reactions, especially when things get tense or uncomfortable. Let’s say you just had a disagreement with a friend. Afterwards, you might ask yourself:
What assumptions did I make about their intentions? Did any strong emotions pop up that changed how I saw the situation? Were there any familiar stories or beliefs swirling around in my mind during that moment?
Journaling can really help here. It gives you space to explore your thoughts and feelings without anyone interrupting. As you keep at it, you’ll start to see patterns—recurring themes or triggers that point to where bias might be influencing you.
Another important piece is learning to notice your emotional cues. Sometimes, your body knows before your mind does. A tightness in your chest, a quick rush of irritation, or that urge to just pull away—these aren’t problems to solve, but signals to get curious about.
Self-awareness also means paying attention to the stories you tell about yourself and the people around you. Are there certain folks you always see as “difficult” or “unreliable”? Or maybe you catch yourself believing you’re not worthy of love or respect? These stories usually come from deeper biases, shaped by old experiences.
Here’s the thing: developing self-awareness is a lifelong practice. It’s not about reaching some final destination. It takes patience, and a lot of compassion—for yourself and for everyone else. But as your awareness grows, something amazing happens: you get to choose how you respond, instead of just reacting on autopilot. And that shift? That’s really at the heart of personal growth, and it’s the key to building healthier, more genuine relationships.

Chapter 4: Empathy and Active Listening as Tools for Bridging Divides.
When you start to really know yourself, something amazing happens—you get the chance to step outside your own perspective and truly connect with others. That’s where empathy comes in. It’s that powerful ability to sense and appreciate what someone else is feeling or going through. And honestly, empathy can be a game-changer. It breaks down the walls that assumptions build and lets us create real, human connections.
Now, here’s the thing—empathy isn’t about agreeing with everything another person says or does. It’s about setting aside your own views, just for a moment, and trying to see the world through their eyes. That takes a bit of humility, and sometimes, a willingness to be changed by what you learn.
Active listening is really where empathy comes to life. Think of it as giving someone your full attention—not just to the words they’re saying, but to their tone, their body language, and all the emotions just under the surface. Instead of focusing on what you’re going to say next, or preparing a rebuttal, you’re just... listening. Really listening.
So, how can you practice active listening? There are a few simple things you can try:
First, keep your body language open. Face the person, make eye contact, and do your best to minimize distractions—put away the phone, turn off the TV. Little things like that show you’re present.
Next, try reflecting the feelings you hear. If someone sounds frustrated, you might say, “It sounds like you’re feeling frustrated.” It’s a small gesture, but it lets them know you’re tuned in.
Don’t be afraid to ask gentle, clarifying questions, either. Something like, “Can you tell me more about what happened?” can encourage someone to open up and share more.
And here’s a big one—resist the urge to fix things right away. Sometimes, people just need space to express themselves without having solutions thrown at them.
Sure, these practices might feel a little awkward at first, especially if you’re used to old patterns. But even small efforts can make a huge difference. When someone feels truly heard, it’s like their defenses just melt away. The whole conversation shifts—from heated debate to genuine dialogue.
There’s something else worth remembering: empathy means understanding that you’ll never fully know what it’s like to walk in someone else’s shoes. But if you bring curiosity and respect to every conversation, you really can start to bridge even the widest divides.
Think about it—in your family, it might mean actually listening to your teenager’s struggles instead of brushing them off as “just a phase.” At work, it could look like seeking out the perspectives of colleagues who’ve had different experiences. And in friendships, it’s about being there for both the highs and the lows, without judging.
Empathy and active listening aren’t quick fixes. They take ongoing effort, and sometimes, a willingness to be a little vulnerable. But these are the real tools that help us overcome bias, and build relationships grounded in trust and mutual respect.

Chapter 5: Practical Strategies for Challenging and Reframing Biased Thinking.
You know, being aware of our biases and developing empathy is a great start. But real change? That happens when we take it a step further—when we actually challenge those old thought patterns and start reshaping them.
So, how do we move from just noticing our biases to actively doing something about them? Well, it’s all about shifting from passive recognition to intentional action. That means questioning your assumptions, opening up to new perspectives, and practicing different ways of thinking.
Here’s a strategy that works surprisingly well—treat your bias like a hypothesis, not a fact. Let's say you feel irritated with a coworker, or maybe you’re suspicious of a new neighbor. Instead of just going with that gut reaction, pause for a moment and ask yourself, “What else could be true?”
It’s such a simple question, but you’ll be amazed at how it opens your mind. Suddenly, you’re not stuck with your first impression—you’re looking for other explanations, and that takes the power away from automatic judgments.
Another powerful approach? Go out of your way to find information or stories that contradict what you already believe. Read articles from different viewpoints. Have a real conversation with someone whose background is totally different from yours. Or think back to a time when your first impression about someone turned out to be completely wrong.
Over time, these little actions chip away at confirmation bias, making room for humility and a more curious mind.
If you want some practical steps for reframing biased thinking, here are a few ideas you can try:
First, identify your triggers. Notice the situations or people that always seem to set you off.
Next, question those automatic thoughts. Don’t just accept the first story your mind comes up with—ask yourself, “What else might be going on?”
Then, practice perspective-taking. Imagine what the situation looks like through someone else’s eyes.
And finally, try using “both/and” thinking. Instead of insisting there’s just one right answer, make room for complexity. Sometimes, more than one thing can be true at the same time.
Now, none of this is about pretending you don’t have feelings, or forcing yourself to be neutral. It’s really about giving yourself more options—about growing and changing, rather than staying stuck.
In your relationships, this might mean you revisit an old argument with a fresh perspective. Maybe you ask yourself, “What was I missing at the time?” or even wonder how your own fears or insecurities might have played a part. Sometimes, it means apologizing for misunderstandings, even if you meant well.
And the more you practice, the more these habits stick. Your mind becomes more flexible, less focused on being right, and more open to learning. Relationships start to feel less like a competition, and more like a journey you’re taking together.
Here’s the truth: challenging bias isn’t something you do just once and forget about. It’s a lifelong journey. You’ll need courage, humility, and a willingness to feel uncomfortable now and then. But the rewards? They’re huge—deeper understanding, stronger connections, and a much greater sense of shared humanity.

Chapter 6: Repairing Relationships After Bias-Driven Conflict
Even when our intentions are good, bias can still sneak in and create tension or distance between us and the people we care about. And honestly, the real sign of growth isn’t about never making mistakes—it’s about how we pick up the pieces and repair after things go wrong. Think of it like tending a garden after a storm. Sometimes, you just have to roll up your sleeves and get to work rebuilding.
So, how do you know when bias has played a role in a misunderstanding or conflict? Sometimes, you’ll feel a lingering tension after a conversation, or maybe you’ll sense that something important was left unsaid. Instead of just moving on, it helps to pause and ask yourself, “Did I make assumptions? Did I really listen? Was I open to being wrong?”
The first real step in repairing is offering a sincere apology—not just for what you said or did, but for how it made the other person feel. This means you actually name the bias or assumption, even if it feels uncomfortable, and let the person know you truly regret the hurt you caused. Imagine saying, “I realize I jumped to conclusions about your intentions, and I’m sorry for not giving you the benefit of the doubt.”
There are a few gentle practices that can really help with relationship repair:
First, own your part. Be clear and honest about how your own bias or reaction played a role in what happened.
Next, invite feedback. Ask the other person how your actions affected them, and listen—really listen—without jumping in to defend yourself.
And finally, make amends. Offer to take a concrete step to rebuild trust. Maybe that’s changing a behavior, or following up with a thoughtful gesture.
Repair isn’t about pretending the past didn’t happen. It’s about building a new kind of trust, one that’s stronger because you worked through something tough together. And it does take patience. Sometimes, the other person just isn’t ready to forgive or reconnect right away. That’s okay. The most important thing is to respect their pace and keep showing up with humility and care.
In families, this might mean having a tough conversation after a heated argument, and being willing to hear some hard truths. In friendships, it could look like reaching out after some time apart, letting them know you truly want to understand and reconnect. And at work? Sometimes it’s about admitting a misstep in a meeting, and then working to create a more inclusive environment from that point forward.
Here’s what’s really powerful: the more you practice repairing, the better you get at it. Every time you mend a relationship, you make it stronger and more resilient. Over time, all those small moments of courage and vulnerability create a culture where honesty and compassion are the norm—and bias has a much harder time taking root.

Chapter 7: Creating Environments That Reduce Bias.
You know, it’s one thing to become aware of our own biases, but have you ever thought about how the spaces we share—at home, at work, or in our communities—can actually make bias easier or harder to challenge?
Think of it like tending a garden. Just as a gardener shapes the soil and light to help things grow, we can design our environments to help us notice and push back against bias.
One of the most powerful ideas here is something called psychological safety. Basically, it’s that feeling you get when you know it’s okay to speak up, to admit you’re unsure, or even to make a mistake—without worrying that you’ll be judged or laughed at.
When people feel safe like this, they’re way more likely to share their honest thoughts, admit when they don’t know something, and actually learn from each other.
So, how do we create these kinds of spaces? Well, here are a few practical ways:
First, set clear norms. That means laying down some ground rules for how we talk to each other—like listening fully, not interrupting, and really valuing everyone’s point of view.
Next, encourage curiosity. What if, instead of treating disagreements like battles, we saw them as chances to learn? Suddenly, debates get a lot less heated—and a lot more interesting.
Modeling vulnerability is huge, too. When leaders or elders admit their own blind spots and ask for feedback, it makes it easier for everyone else to do the same.
And don’t forget about diversifying voices. Go out of your way to include people with different backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives. It’s amazing what happens when you broaden the conversation.
Let’s make this real. In families, it could mean setting aside time for open conversations, where everyone gets to speak up. At work, maybe it’s structured feedback sessions, or even anonymous suggestion boxes so people feel safer sharing their ideas. And in our communities, think about events that celebrate all kinds of cultures and encourage people to connect with someone new.
Now, I won’t pretend these environments are always comfortable. In fact, when you invite honest conversations, you might run into conflict or dig up issues that have been hiding beneath the surface. But here’s the thing—over time, these spaces become stronger, more creative, and more connected.
The real aim isn’t to wipe out every bit of bias—let’s be honest, that’s just not possible. Instead, we want to build places where bias doesn’t go unnoticed, and where everyone feels empowered to question it, together.

Chapter 8: Sustaining Growth Through Ongoing Practice
Overcoming bias isn’t something you check off a list—it’s really a lifelong journey. Think of it a bit like learning to play the guitar, or picking up a new language. It takes steady effort, a lot of patience, and the willingness to begin again, even when you slip up.
Sustaining real growth means making awareness, empathy, and repair part of your everyday life.
Here’s a helpful way to picture it: imagine bias work as your “mental fitness routine.” Just like you keep your body healthy with small, consistent habits, you keep your mind flexible and open with regular practice. So, what does that look like in real life?
Maybe it’s taking a few moments each day to reflect—just pausing and noticing when assumptions or biases pop up, and gently asking yourself where they might come from.
Or, you might set aside time each week to check in with a friend, a partner, or a group you trust. Share your challenges, your insights, and learn from each other.
Another powerful habit is inviting feedback. What if you could ask people to point out blindspots you might not see? And when they do, try meeting it with gratitude instead of getting defensive.
And of course, everyone makes mistakes. The key is to treat those moments as chances to grow, not as reasons to feel ashamed.
Here’s something we often forget: it’s important to celebrate progress, no matter how small. Did a conversation go a little smoother than usual? Did you welcome a new perspective, even if it challenged you? Those moments matter. Over time, they build up, creating real momentum and a sense of what’s possible.
Being gentle with yourself is part of this, too. Bias runs deep, and old habits can sneak back in, especially when you’re tired or stressed. When that happens, it’s okay to return to the basics—pause, reflect, and reconnect with empathy. Every day gives you a fresh start to practice.
In our relationships, this steady effort creates trust and safety. People start to feel seen and valued, even when they don’t agree on everything. In our communities, it helps build a culture of curiosity and respect.
The truth is, the journey never really ends. But every step you take brings a deeper sense of understanding—and a stronger connection to those around you.

Chapter 9: Navigating Cultural and Systemic Bias.
You know, a lot of the work in overcoming bias happens one-on-one, or even within ourselves. But there’s something bigger at play too—those powerful cultural and systemic forces that shape the way we see the world.
Bias isn’t just personal. It’s woven deep into the structures and stories all around us. Think about cultural bias—it pops up in the media we watch, the history we learn, and even the unspoken rules about what’s considered “normal.” Systemic bias? That’s built right into policies, institutions, and everyday practices—quietly giving an advantage to some, while making things tougher for others.
The tricky part? These bigger forces can actually reinforce our own blindspots, making it really tough to spot them, let alone challenge them.
So, how do you start navigating all this? First, it takes both awareness and action. Here are a few practical steps that make a real difference:
Start by educating yourself. Seek out books, films, and conversations that bring new perspectives—stories and histories you might not have heard before.
Next, question the norms around you. Notice whose voices are always heard, and ask yourself—whose stories are missing from the conversation?
Advocate for change, both close to home and out in the world. Support policies and practices that make things fairer and more inclusive, whether it’s in your friend group, your workplace, or your community.
And don’t go it alone. Build alliances—connect with others who care about challenging bias, and work together. Real change is always stronger as a team effort.
I know, this can feel overwhelming, especially when you’re facing deep-rooted injustices or beliefs that have been around forever. But here’s something to remember—small steps count. Every time you question a stereotype, retell a story from a different point of view, or welcome a new voice into the mix, you’re helping to gently reweave the fabric of society.
What does this look like in real life? In families, it might mean honest talks about privilege and difference. At work, maybe it’s about reviewing hiring practices or creating mentorships for those who’ve been left out. And in your neighborhood, it could be as simple as supporting local groups that celebrate diversity and push for inclusion.
Addressing cultural and systemic bias isn’t about pointing fingers or feeling guilty. It’s about shared responsibility. When we work together, even the smallest actions can add up—moving us closer to a world that’s just a little more fair, and a whole lot more compassionate.

Chapter 10: Integrating Bias Awareness Into Everyday Life.
So, here we are at the final step—bringing bias awareness into the ebb and flow of our daily lives. Instead of sticking to a strict playbook, it’s really about shifting your mindset. Imagine living with more openness, humility, and a genuine sense of curiosity.
Integration isn’t just about what happens during big disagreements. It’s about those tiny, everyday moments—like, who do you greet with real warmth? Whose ideas do you actually listen to? Whose stories do you believe without hesitation? Sometimes, it means pausing and quietly asking yourself, “What might I be missing here?”—even when everything seems to be just fine.
Want a few gentle reminders to help make this part of your routine?
First, stay curious. Treat every conversation like a chance to discover something new—even if it’s small.
Next, practice gratitude. Take a moment to appreciate all the different perspectives and experiences swirling around you each day.
Extend grace—not just to others, but to yourself too. When bias pops up, see it as an opportunity to grow, not a reason to be hard on yourself.
And finally, commit to the journey. Overcoming bias isn’t a box you check off—it’s a lifelong process, and every step you take really does matter.
Here’s something to remember: integration isn’t about being perfect. We all have blindspots, and there will be moments when we misunderstand each other. But if you move through your days with intention and a little extra care, you’ll start building relationships—and even communities—founded on honesty, empathy, and real respect.

As we wrap up, let's take a moment to bring all of this together. Overcoming unconscious bias and building better relationships isn't a straight path—it's more like a winding journey filled with self-discovery, humility, and a whole lot of growth. Think about the steps we've explored: noticing those hidden patterns, understanding how bias sneaks into conversations, building your own self-awareness, practicing empathy, challenging your assumptions, making things right when conflict happens, shaping supportive spaces, keeping up with the work, taking on bigger systems, and really weaving this awareness into your daily life. Together, these aren't just steps—they form a living, breathing way to create real change.
So, what does all this mean for you? First off, bias is just part of being human—it doesn't make you a bad person. The real magic happens when you pair self-awareness with empathy. When you repair relationships after bias-driven conflict, that's how trust and resilience grow. And honestly, it's so much easier to notice and challenge bias when you're surrounded by people who support you. Most importantly, lasting growth comes from gentle, ongoing practice and a little self-compassion.
Remember, it's not about being perfect or erasing every bit of bias. It's about learning to see more clearly, to listen with an open heart, and to respond with kindness and curiosity. There'll be uncomfortable moments, and sometimes old habits will come back. When that happens, just go back to the basics: pause, reflect, and reach out with empathy.
You don't have to walk this path alone. Every small act of awareness, every honest conversation, every time you mend a relationship—they all add up. These little efforts ripple out, touching families, workplaces, and entire communities. Change rarely happens overnight, but it does happen—one person, one moment at a time.
So as you move forward, carry these ideas gently. Let them shape how you connect, guide your choices, and remind you that growth is always possible. With patience, a bit of courage, and plenty of compassion, you really can help create the kind of relationships—and the kind of world—where everyone feels like they truly belong.
